analysis.one_liner: Creates government health insurance for every child and pregnant woman, funded by a new payroll tax.
analysis.headline: A bill to give every child and pregnant woman public health coverage with no deductibles or copays died in committee after drawing one sponsor and zero cosponsors, and was never voted on.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new public health insurance program covering every child in the country from birth through age 22, plus all pregnancy-related care for every woman. Benefits would mirror Medicare's hospital and doctor coverage, and well-child visits, immunizations, prenatal care, and delivery would come with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments. It would be paid for by a new payroll tax of 1.45% taken from workers' wages and 1.45% charged to employers, with the self-employed paying 2.9%.
analysis.who_benefits: Every child in the United States through age 22 and every woman during pregnancy and 60 days after would gain free public health coverage, including well-child care, immunizations, preventive dental care, prenatal care, delivery, and postnatal family planning with no out-of-pocket costs. Families with employer coverage could keep their children on the public plan, since the program pays before private plans. Doctors and hospitals would gain millions of new paying patients, plus a 5% payment bonus for women who start prenatal care in the first trimester.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a new public health insurance program under which every child from birth to age 23 and every pregnant woman is entitled to coverage, with no premiums mentioned in the entitlement itself.

Gives children the same benefit package as Medicare Part A and Part B, and adds well-baby care, routine office visits, immunizations (including the vaccines themselves), routine lab tests, and preventive dental care with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments.

Covers prenatal care, inpatient labor and delivery, postnatal care, and postnatal family planning for all women with no cost-sharing, and pays doctors a 5% bonus for patients who begin prenatal care in the first trimester.

Discourages medically unnecessary surgery by paying 95% of the normal rate for cesarean sections and by requiring peer review organization approval before non-routine pregnancy services are delivered.

analysis.who_pays: All employers would pay a new 1.45% excise tax on wages, workers would pay a new 1.45% tax on their wages, and self-employed people would pay 2.9% on their business income, starting after December 31, 1992. The money would flow into a new Children and Mothers Health Insurance Trust Fund. Private health insurers would lose the children's and maternity portions of the coverage market, since the public program pays before group health plans.

drawbacks.text: The program would be financed by a new 2.9% combined payroll tax — 1.45% from workers and 1.45% from employers, 2.9% for the self-employed — a broad tax on wages that raises the cost of employment and, because it applies only to wages, weighs more heavily on working people than an income-tax increase would.

The bill makes the new program the primary payer ahead of group health plans, so employers and insurers would have a strong incentive to stop covering dependents and shift children and maternity care onto the public plan, increasing the program's cost beyond projections.

Non-routine pregnancy services would require advance approval from a peer review organization before they could be billed, adding a layer of bureaucratic review between patients and their doctors in urgent or complicated situations outside the routine-care exception.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and real: universal, no-cost-sharing coverage for every child and pregnancy would have eliminated a major category of uninsured Americans at the height of the early-1990s coverage crisis. The cost is also large: a permanent 2.9% payroll tax on all wages, which lands on both workers and employers and is a blunter instrument than progressive income taxation. The design borrowed Medicare's fee-for-service machinery wholesale — carriers, intermediaries, hospital payment rules — which would have meant huge new claims volume processed through an existing bureaucracy, and the primary-payer rule invited employers to drop dependent coverage. An honest supporter would acknowledge the tax burden on middle-income workers and the risk that public costs grew as private coverage retreated; an honest opponent would have to concede that the bill guaranteed coverage for every child and pregnancy in the country.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in May 1991, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Represent Pete Stark introduced the bill on May 16, 1991, and it was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

On May 22, 1991, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and the record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 102nd Congress — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
Under the bill's own terms, no benefits could have been paid for services before January 1, 1993, and the Congress expired before that date, ending the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and employers came out ahead: no new 1.45% payroll tax on employers was ever imposed, and insurers kept the children's and maternity portions of the private coverage market that the bill would have moved into a public program. Children and pregnant women without adequate coverage remained uncovered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers that avoided the tax

for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), member of the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its entire sponsorship; no cosponsor ever joined.

against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: the bill was sent to the Health Subcommittee on May 22, 1991, and the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Every other member of the House
against.what_they_did: None signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with a single sponsor and no visible bloc of support to push it through committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, and the only record of support is one Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so the bill never revealed whether it had partisan backing beyond its author.

industries.note: The bill would move all children and all maternity care into a public program that pays before group health plans, stripping insurers of that portion of the market and the premiums that come with it. Insurers losing this business is a direct cost of the coverage the bill offered families.

Every employer would owe a new 1.45% excise tax on wages to fund the program. Many employers would also face pressure to drop dependent coverage, since the public program would pay first for children and maternity care.

Doctors and hospitals would gain millions of newly covered, paying patients with no cost-sharing barriers, and a 5% bonus for early prenatal care. Against that, cesarean payments would be cut to 95% of the normal rate and non-routine maternity services would need advance approval from peer review organizations.

The bill extends Medicare's section 1876 contracting rules to the new program, letting HMOs enroll covered children, but pregnant women could be served only under cost-reimbursement contracts rather than risk contracts, limiting the more lucrative arrangement pending a further study report.
